first.rationale: Onboarding completion is down 4% QoQ and activation is down 6% QoQ—both metrics point to friction in the early user journey. Memory_31 and memory_86 show that simplification and shortening onboarding have produced durable activation lifts in SMB segments. Memory_91 (activation messaging) provides a complementary signal. Promotional pricing (memory_73) addresses the competitive threat but risks margin compression and may not address the underlying activation friction driving the 6% decline. Referral incentives work best on established customers, not solving current onboarding/activation deterioration. Enterprise sales assist is orthogonal to the SMB activation problem. Verifying memory_31 (signup simplification) and memory_73 (promotional pricing effectiveness) will clarify whether onboarding simplification is sufficiently supported vs. whether pricing pressure is the primary lever. A standard_experiment on simplified onboarding targets the measurable metric deterioration, preserves optionality on pricing response, and aligns with the primary objective of sustainable qualified revenue by improving conversion quality rather than competing on price.

final.rationale: Verification confirms the critical distinction: memory_31 showed signup +15%, activation +9%, qualified revenue +4% with only -1% retention hit on SMB. Memory_73 revealed that promotional pricing drives short-term signup (+31%) and revenue (+18%) but destroys cohort durability with -12% retention loss—unsustainable against the primary objective of long-term qualified revenue. The current situation shows activation down 6% and onboarding completion down 4%, both pointing to friction in the self-serve journey rather than price sensitivity as the binding constraint. Simplifying onboarding directly addresses these measurable declines, leverages proven SMB mechanics from memory_31, and compounds with activation messaging (memory_91) and shortened flows (memory_86). This preserves margin, improves cohort quality, and avoids the retention cliff demonstrated by discounting. Promotional pricing would be a false solution to what is fundamentally a conversion/friction problem, not a willingness-to-pay problem.
